paper_context.research_question: How can open information extraction systems produce minimized, non-redundant extractions while retaining semantic information through structured annotations, and what is the trade-off between extraction brevity and precision/recall?
contribution_style: incremental improvement over prior work (ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE)
explicit handling of linguistic phenomena (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities)
main_claims: Overly-specific extractions in OIE can be systematically reduced by identifying and removing specific constituents while preserving meaning through annotations
Polarity, modality, attribution, and quantity information can be reliably extracted and represented as annotations rather than embedded in extraction text
Multiple minimization modes (safe, frequency, collocations, aggressive) enable trade-offs between extraction brevity and precision
MinIE achieves competitive or higher precision and recall than prior systems (ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE) while producing significantly shorter extractions
Negative polarity annotations address a critical gap in prior OIE systems regarding absence of negative evidence
Redundant extractions from underlying systems can be consolidated through minimization without loss of information
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Factual precision: fraction of correct triples accounting for factuality annotations
Attribution precision: correctness of supplier and factuality information in attributions
Recall: total number of extractions and non-redundant extractions produced
Extraction length: mean word count and standard deviation as proxy for minimality
Redundancy analysis: comparison of redundant vs. non-redundant extractions across systems
Mode-specific trade-offs: precision/recall degradation across safe, frequency, collocations, and aggressive modes
Annotation coverage: frequency of polarity, modality, attribution, and quantity annotations
Error analysis: sources of errors (dependency parsing, collocation handling, NER failures)
Downstream task utility: implicit evaluation through application to IR, QA, KB extension

extracted_claims.claim_text: Overly-specific extractions in OIE can be systematically reduced by identifying and removing specific constituents while preserving meaning through annotations
evidence: Table 1 demonstrates minimization of 'Pinocchio believes that the hero Superman was not actually born on beautiful Krypton' across systems
MinIE rewrites extractions by (1) identifying and removing overly specific parts and (2) representing polarity, modality, attribution, quantities as annotations
Section 5 describes basic minimization techniques for polarity, modality, attribution, quantities
uncertainty_flags: No formal definition of 'overly specific' provided; relies on intuitive linguistic judgment
Preservation of meaning is asserted but not formally validated against semantic equivalence metrics
Annotation scheme's sufficiency for capturing removed information not proven

extracted_claims.claim_text: Polarity, modality, attribution, and quantity information can be reliably extracted and represented as annotations rather than embedded in extraction text
evidence: Section 5.1: Negation detection via lexicon of {no, not, never, none}; assigns polarity annotation
Section 5.2: Modality detection via modal verbs, possibility-indicating words, infinitive phrases
Section 5.3: Attribution extraction from subordinate clauses and 'according to' patterns
Section 5.4: Quantity detection via NER (NUMBER, PERCENT) and quantity words (all, some, many)
Table 3 shows annotation coverage: 10.7% attributions, 3.7% negative polarity, 9.9% possibility, 17.8% quantities
uncertainty_flags: Negation detection explicitly limited to 'easy cases'; acknowledges negation scope, focus, double negation not handled (line 497-499)
Modality approach uses only CT/PS levels; authors note more advanced approaches exist (Saurí & Pustejovsky 2012)
Attribution detection limited to subordinate clauses and 'according to' patterns; may miss other attribution sources
Quantity detection relies on NER quality; no error analysis provided for quantity extraction
No inter-annotator agreement or reliability metrics reported for annotation correctness

extracted_claims.claim_text: Multiple minimization modes (safe, frequency, collocations, aggressive) enable trade-offs between extraction brevity and precision
evidence: Section 6.1: MinIE-S (safe mode) drops only universally safe constituents (determiners, possessives, adverbs modifying verbs)
Section 6.2: MinIE-F and MinIE-C use dictionary D of stable constituents; differ in dictionary source
Section 6.3: MinIE-A (aggressive) drops all adverbial, adjective, possessive, temporal modifiers recursively
Table 3 shows extraction length decreases across modes: MinIE-S (7.2±4.2) → MinIE-F (6.9±4.0) → MinIE-C (6.8±4.0) → MinIE-A (4.7±1.9)
Table 4 shows precision degradation: MinIE-S (0.79) → MinIE-F (0.78) → MinIE-C (0.78) → MinIE-A (0.68) on NYT
uncertainty_flags: Trade-off curve not formally characterized; no Pareto frontier analysis
Precision drop between MinIE-S and MinIE-A is substantial (0.79 to 0.68) but authors note 'surprisingly' still higher than Stanford OIE
Mode selection criteria not specified; no guidance on choosing mode for downstream applications
Frequency threshold (≥10) for MinIE-F appears arbitrary; sensitivity analysis not provided

extracted_claims.claim_text: MinIE achieves competitive or higher precision and recall than prior systems (ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE) while producing significantly shorter extractions
evidence: Table 4 (NYT): MinIE-S factual precision 0.79 vs ClausIE 0.68, OLLIE 0.71, Stanford 0.62
Table 4 (Wiki): MinIE-S factual precision 0.83 vs ClausIE 0.73, OLLIE 0.71, Stanford 0.54
Table 3: MinIE extraction lengths (4.7-7.2 words) significantly shorter than ClausIE (10.9±7) and comparable to Stanford (6.6±3.0)
Recall (non-redundant extractions): MinIE-S 623/791 (NYT) vs ClausIE 621/928, OLLIE 306/435
uncertainty_flags: Recall measured as 'non-redundant extractions' but redundancy definition is simplistic (subsequence matching only)
Total extraction count shows MinIE sometimes produces fewer extractions than ClausIE; authors attribute to consolidation of redundant extractions but this is not independently verified
Precision evaluation limited to 200-sentence samples (NYT, Wiki); statistical significance not reported
Attribution precision numbers based on small sample (most sentences lack attributions); authors acknowledge 'should be taken with a grain of salt'
Comparison to Stanford OIE may be unfair: Stanford OIE produces many redundant variants; when redundancy discounted, comparison becomes less clear

extracted_claims.claim_text: Negative polarity annotations address a critical gap in prior OIE systems regarding absence of negative evidence
evidence: Lines 119-125: 'The absence of negative evidence is a major concern for reasoning with OIE extractions' citing Dong et al. (2014), Riedel et al. (2013), Petroni et al. (2015)
MinIE is claimed to be 'first OIE system to produce such negative-polarity extractions' (line 118)
Table 1 shows MinIE extracts (Superman, was born on, Krypton) with annotation fact(- [not], CT) from negated sentence
Table 3: 3.7% of extractions have negative polarity annotation
uncertainty_flags: Claim that prior systems lack negative evidence not empirically demonstrated in paper
Negative polarity coverage (3.7%) is low; unclear if this represents true negation frequency in text or detection limitations
No evaluation of downstream utility of negative polarity annotations for reasoning tasks
Negation detection limited to relation-level negations; subject/argument negations missed (acknowledged line 497-499)

extracted_claims.claim_text: Redundant extractions from underlying systems can be consolidated through minimization without loss of information
evidence: Table 3: ClausIE produces 58,420 total extractions but only 41,174 non-redundant; MinIE-S produces 45,649 total but 37,638 non-redundant
Authors note: 'different (partly redundant) extractions from ClausIE may lead to the same minimized extraction' (line 720)
Stanford OIE produces many extraction variants by dropping different subsets of words, creating redundancy
uncertainty_flags: Redundancy definition is simplistic: 't1 redundant if it appears as subsequence in some other triple t2' (line 755-756)
This definition may miss semantic redundancy (e.g., paraphrases, near-duplicates)
No analysis of information loss from consolidation; claim that consolidation preserves information not validated
Unclear whether minimization actually causes consolidation or merely reveals pre-existing redundancy in ClausIE output

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Dependency parsing is sufficiently accurate for OIE minimization
supporting_evidence: MinIE relies on ClausIE, which uses dependency parsing
Authors acknowledge: 'For all modes, errors in dependency parsing transfer over to errors in MinIE, which we believe is the main source of errors in MinIE-S' (line 801-803)
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Parsing errors propagate through minimization pipeline, degrading precision. Authors identify this as primary error source but do not quantify impact or propose mitigation.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Clause-based extraction is sufficient for OIE
supporting_evidence: MinIE 'focuses on extractions obtained from individual clauses (with the exception of attribution)' (line 303-304)
Architecture processes each clause independently via ClausIE
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Cross-clause relations and complex sentence structures may be missed or incorrectly decomposed. Paper does not evaluate performance on complex multi-clause sentences.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Negation detection via lexicon {no, not, never, none} is sufficient
supporting_evidence: Simple lexicon-based approach used for negation detection
Authors acknowledge: 'negation detection is a hard problem and involves questions such as negation scope resolution, focus detection, and double negation' (line 497-499)
Authors state: 'MinIE does not address these problems, but restricts attention to the easy cases' (line 499-500)
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Negation scope errors, focus misattribution, and double negation handling failures. Authors acknowledge but do not quantify frequency or impact.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Modality can be represented with binary CT/PS distinction
supporting_evidence: Modality represented as CT (certainty) or PS (possibility) only
Authors note: 'A more advanced approach is taken by (Saurí and Pustejovsky, 2012)' (line 480)
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Fine-grained modality distinctions (e.g., degrees of likelihood) are lost. Downstream applications requiring nuanced modality may suffer.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Collocations from WordNet and Wiktionary are domain-independent and sufficient
supporting_evidence: MinIE-C uses 'all multi-word expressions from WordNet and Wiktionary, which we consider domain-independent' (line 580-581)

Authors acknowledge: 'In practice, applications can extend the dictionary using suitable collocations, either from domain-dependent dictionaries or by using methods to automatically extract collocations from a text corpus' (line 581-583)
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Domain-specific collocations are missed, leading to incorrect minimization (e.g., 'assistant director' broken into 'director'). Authors identify this error source (line 809-811) but do not quantify frequency.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Frequency threshold ≥10 for MinIE-F is appropriate
supporting_evidence: MinIE-F includes 'all frequent (e.g., frequency ≥ 10) subjects, relations, and arguments into D' (line 587-588)
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Threshold may be too low (over-minimization) or too high (under-minimization) for different domains or text types. No sensitivity analysis provided.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Subsequence-based redundancy definition captures meaningful redundancy
supporting_evidence: Redundancy defined as: 't1 redundant if it appears as subsequence in some other triple t2 produced by the same extractor from the same sentence' (line 755-756)
Example: extraction 5 in Table 1 is redundant given extraction 6
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Semantic redundancy (paraphrases, near-duplicates) not captured. Recall metrics may be misleading if non-redundant extractions are semantically similar.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Factual precision metric (entailment-based) is appropriate for OIE evaluation
supporting_evidence: Triple labeled correct if 'entailed by its corresponding clause; here factuality annotations are taken into account' (line 738-739)
Example: 'all triples except #3 of Tab. 1 are considered correct' (line 740)
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Entailment-based evaluation may not capture utility for downstream tasks (IR, QA, KB extension). No downstream task evaluation provided.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Mean word count is a valid proxy for minimality
supporting_evidence: Authors measure 'mean word count per extraction (µ) and its standard deviation (σ); we use these numbers as a proxy for minimality' (line 751-752)
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Word count may not correlate with semantic minimality. Extractions with fewer words may retain redundant information; longer extractions may be more informative.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: ClausIE is a suitable foundation for MinIE
supporting_evidence: MinIE built on ClausIE because: '(1) it separates the identification of the constituents of the extractions from the generation of propositions, (2) it detects clause types, which are also useful for MinIE, and (3) it is a state-of-the-art OIE system' (line 305-308)
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: MinIE's performance is bounded by ClausIE's quality. Improvements to ClausIE may not transfer to MinIE if minimization introduces new errors.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: MinIE presents a methodologically sound engineering contribution to open information extraction that systematically addresses extraction minimization through constituent removal and annotation-based representation. The paper's logical structure is well-organized: it motivates the problem (overly-specific extractions), proposes a multi-mode solution (Safe/Frequency/Collocations/Aggressive), implements it on ClausIE, and evaluates empirically. The core argument chain is coherent: (1) OIE systems produce overly-specific extractions → (2) minimization via constituent removal + annotations preserves meaning → (3) multiple modes enable precision/brevity trade-offs → (4) empirical results show competitive performance with shorter extractions. However, the reasoning exhibits controlled weaknesses in formalization, scope limitations, and evaluation depth. The paper acknowledges many limitations explicitly (negation scope, modality granularity, collocation handling, clause-based extraction), which strengthens transparency but also reveals the incremental nature of the contribution. The annotation scheme is novel for OIE (particularly negative polarity), but the minimization techniques are largely engineering refinements of prior work (ReVerb, Stanford OIE, OLLIE). The empirical evaluation is solid but limited in scale (200-sentence labeled samples) and lacks downstream task validation. The paper's logical coherence is high within its stated scope, but the scope itself is narrow and the innovation is primarily in system design rather than conceptual breakthrough.
logical_argument_graph: Problem motivation: OIE systems produce overly-specific extractions (e.g., 'the hero Superman' instead of 'Superman') that reduce utility for downstream tasks
Root cause: Lack of systematic minimization techniques that preserve semantic information while reducing verbosity
Proposed solution: MinIE rewrites extractions via (1) constituent removal and (2) annotation-based representation of polarity, modality, attribution, quantities
Design principle: Multiple minimization modes (Safe→Frequency→Collocations→Aggressive) enable tunable trade-offs between brevity and precision
Implementation strategy: Build on ClausIE (clause-based extraction) and enrich with annotation framework
Annotation sufficiency claim: Polarity, modality, attribution, quantity annotations capture removed information without loss of meaning
Empirical validation: Comparative evaluation shows MinIE achieves competitive/higher precision than ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE while producing shorter extractions
Redundancy consolidation: Minimization consolidates redundant extractions from underlying systems (verified via subsequence-based redundancy definition)
Critical gap addressed: Negative polarity annotations address absence of negative evidence in prior OIE systems (cited as major concern for reasoning)
Limitation acknowledgment: Negation detection restricted to 'easy cases'; scope/focus/double-negation not handled; clause-based extraction may miss cross-clause relations

identified_claims.claim_text: Overly-specific extractions in OIE can be systematically reduced by identifying and removing specific constituents while preserving meaning through annotations
evidence: Table 1 demonstrates minimization pipeline: input extraction → basic extraction (polarity/modality/attribution/quantity removed) → minimized extraction (additional constituents dropped)
Section 5 describes basic minimization techniques for polarity (5.1), modality (5.2), attribution (5.3), quantities (5.4) with corresponding annotations
Section 6 describes four minimization modes with increasing aggressiveness, each with defined stable subconstituents

Example: 'Pinocchio believes that the hero Superman was not actually born on beautiful Krypton' → (Superman, was born on, Krypton) with annotations fact(- [not], CT), attribution(Pinocchio, +, PS [believes])
uncertainty_flags: No formal definition of 'overly specific' provided; relies on intuitive linguistic judgment and domain-independent heuristics
Preservation of meaning asserted but not formally validated against semantic equivalence metrics (e.g., entailment, paraphrase similarity)
Annotation scheme's sufficiency for capturing removed information not proven; relies on assumption that annotations are complete and non-redundant
No evaluation of whether downstream tasks (IR, QA, KB extension) actually benefit from minimized + annotated extractions vs. original extractions

identified_claims.claim_text: Polarity, modality, attribution, and quantity information can be reliably extracted and represented as annotations rather than embedded in extraction text
evidence: Section 5.1: Negation detection via lexicon {no, not, never, none}; assigns polarity annotation; Table 2 shows examples
Section 5.2: Modality detection via modal verbs (may, can), possibility-indicating words (probably, possibly), infinitive phrases (is going to); uses CT/PS binary
Section 5.3: Attribution extraction from subordinate clauses (ccomp dependency) and 'according to' patterns; includes supplier and factuality (polarity + modality)
Section 5.4: Quantity detection via NER (NUMBER, PERCENT) and quantity words (all, some, many); replaces with placeholder Q
Table 3 shows annotation coverage: 10.7% attributions, 3.7% negative polarity, 9.9% possibility, 17.8% quantities on NYT-10k
uncertainty_flags: Negation detection explicitly limited to 'easy cases'; acknowledges negation scope, focus, double negation not handled (lines 497-499)
Modality approach uses only CT/PS binary levels; authors note more advanced approaches exist (Saurí & Pustejovsky 2012) but not explored
Attribution detection limited to subordinate clauses (ccomp) and 'according to' patterns; may miss other attribution sources (e.g., parenthetical attributions, implicit attributions)
Quantity detection relies on NER quality; no error analysis provided for quantity extraction accuracy; placeholder approach may lose semantic nuance (e.g., 'almost 10' vs. 'exactly 10')
No inter-annotator agreement or reliability metrics reported for annotation correctness; no human evaluation of annotation quality
Annotation coverage is low for negations (3.7%); unclear if this represents true negation frequency in text or detection limitations

identified_claims.claim_text: Multiple minimization modes (safe, frequency, collocations, aggressive) enable trade-offs between extraction brevity and precision
evidence: Section 6.1: MinIE-S (safe mode) drops only universally safe constituents (determiners, possessives, adverbs modifying verbs, adjectives/adverbials modifying persons)
Section 6.2: MinIE-F and MinIE-C use dictionary D of stable constituents; differ in dictionary source (frequency ≥10 vs. WordNet+Wiktionary)
Section 6.3: MinIE-A (aggressive) drops all adverbial, adjective, possessive, temporal modifiers recursively
Table 3 shows extraction length decreases across modes: MinIE-S (7.2±4.2) → MinIE-F (6.9±4.0) → MinIE-C (6.8±4.0) → MinIE-A (4.7±1.9) on NYT-10k
Table 4 shows precision degradation: MinIE-S (0.79) → MinIE-F (0.78) → MinIE-C (0.78) → MinIE-A (0.68) on NYT
uncertainty_flags: Trade-off curve not formally characterized; no Pareto frontier analysis or explicit precision-recall-length trade-off curves

Precision drop between MinIE-S and MinIE-A is substantial (0.79 to 0.68, 11.4% relative drop) but authors note 'surprisingly' still higher than Stanford OIE (0.62); fairness of comparison unclear given Stanford's redundancy generation
Mode selection criteria not specified; no guidance on choosing mode for downstream applications; users must manually select based on their precision/brevity preferences
Frequency threshold (≥10) for MinIE-F appears arbitrary; no sensitivity analysis provided; unclear how threshold affects performance on different domains or text types
Minimal precision difference between MinIE-F and MinIE-C (0.78 vs 0.78) despite different dictionary sources; suggests dictionary choice may not be critical, but this is not analyzed

identified_claims.claim_text: MinIE achieves competitive or higher precision and recall than prior systems (ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE) while producing significantly shorter extractions
evidence: Table 4 (NYT): MinIE-S factual precision 0.79 vs ClausIE 0.68, OLLIE 0.71, Stanford 0.62 (on 200-sentence sample)
Table 4 (Wiki): MinIE-S factual precision 0.83 vs ClausIE 0.73, OLLIE 0.71, Stanford 0.54 (on 200-sentence sample)
Table 3: MinIE extraction lengths (4.7-7.2 words) significantly shorter than ClausIE (10.9±7) and comparable to Stanford (6.6±3.0) on NYT-10k
Table 3: Recall (non-redundant extractions): MinIE-S 37,638/45,649 vs ClausIE 41,174/58,420, OLLIE 21,277/24,316 on NYT-10k
Section 7.3: 'MinIE-S had higher precision than ClausIE' (line 773-774); authors attribute to implicit extractions, extraction length reduction, and CoreNLP version differences
uncertainty_flags: Recall measured as 'non-redundant extractions' but redundancy definition is simplistic (subsequence matching only); semantic redundancy (paraphrases, near-duplicates) not captured

Total extraction count shows MinIE sometimes produces fewer extractions than ClausIE; authors attribute to consolidation of redundant extractions but this is not independently verified (no analysis of which ClausIE redundancies are consolidated)
Precision evaluation limited to 200-sentence samples (NYT, Wiki); statistical significance not reported; no confidence intervals or p-values provided
Attribution precision numbers based on sparse data (most sentences lack attributions); authors acknowledge 'should be taken with a grain of salt' (line 777); reliability unclear

Comparison to Stanford OIE may be unfair: Stanford OIE produces many redundant variants; when redundancy discounted, comparison becomes less clear (Stanford has 16,779 non-redundant vs 43,365 total extractions)
MinIE-S precision (0.79) is higher than ClausIE (0.68), but MinIE is built on ClausIE; improvement may come from implicit extractions or CoreNLP version, not minimization itself
No statistical significance testing; small sample sizes (200 sentences) may not support strong claims about superiority

identified_claims.claim_text: Negative polarity annotations address a critical gap in prior OIE systems regarding absence of negative evidence
evidence: Lines 119-125: 'The absence of negative evidence is a major concern for reasoning with OIE extractions' citing Dong et al. (2014), Riedel et al. (2013), Petroni et al. (2015)
MinIE is claimed to be 'first OIE system to produce such negative-polarity extractions' (line 118)
Table 1 shows MinIE extracts (Superman, was born on, Krypton) with annotation fact(- [not], CT) from negated sentence
Table 3: 3.7% of extractions have negative polarity annotation on NYT-10k
uncertainty_flags: Claim that prior systems lack negative evidence not empirically demonstrated in paper; no comparison of how ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE handle negations
Negative polarity coverage (3.7%) is low; unclear if this represents true negation frequency in text or detection limitations; no analysis of false negatives
No evaluation of downstream utility of negative polarity annotations for reasoning tasks (KB extension, QA, etc.); claim of 'critical gap' not validated empirically

Negation detection limited to relation-level negations; subject/argument negations missed (acknowledged line 497-499); example given: 'No people were hurt' extracts (Q1 people, were hurt, fire) instead of (people, were hurt, fire) with negative polarity
No comparison to how other systems might represent negations (e.g., Stanford OIE may include 'not' in relation); unclear if MinIE's approach is truly novel or just a different representation

identified_claims.claim_text: Redundant extractions from underlying systems can be consolidated through minimization without loss of information
evidence: Table 3: ClausIE produces 58,420 total extractions but only 41,174 non-redundant; MinIE-S produces 45,649 total but 37,638 non-redundant on NYT-10k
Authors note: 'different (partly redundant) extractions from ClausIE may lead to the same minimized extraction' (line 720)
Stanford OIE produces many extraction variants by dropping different subsets of words, creating redundancy (line 721-722)
uncertainty_flags: Redundancy definition is simplistic: 't1 redundant if it appears as subsequence in some other triple t2' (line 755-756); this definition may miss semantic redundancy (e.g., paraphrases, near-duplicates with different word order)

No analysis of information loss from consolidation; claim that consolidation preserves information not validated; unclear if minimized extractions actually capture all information from redundant originals

Unclear whether minimization actually causes consolidation or merely reveals pre-existing redundancy in ClausIE output; no analysis of which ClausIE redundancies are consolidated by which minimization modes

Comparison of redundancy rates: ClausIE 41,174/58,420 (70.5% non-redundant) vs MinIE-S 37,638/45,649 (82.4% non-redundant); improvement is modest and may be due to fewer total extractions rather than consolidation
No evaluation of whether consolidated extractions are actually more useful for downstream tasks

strengths.title: Well-motivated problem with clear practical relevance
strengths.description: The paper identifies a genuine problem in OIE: overly-specific extractions that reduce utility for downstream tasks. The motivating example (Table 1) effectively demonstrates the issue across multiple systems and clearly shows how MinIE addresses it through minimization and annotations.
evidence: Introduction (lines 001-050) provides clear motivation with concrete example
Table 1 shows extractions from multiple systems on same sentence, making problem visible
Downstream task relevance cited: IR, QA, KB extension (lines 001-010)

strengths.title: Comprehensive annotation framework for OIE
strengths.description: MinIE introduces a structured annotation scheme (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) that is more expressive than prior work (OLLIE). The annotation framework is well-designed and captures important semantic information that would otherwise be lost during minimization. This is a genuine contribution to OIE representation.
evidence: Section 5 describes four annotation types with clear semantics
Table 2 shows examples of factuality annotations with polarity and modality
Table 3 shows annotation coverage across modes
Comparison to OLLIE (lines 201-230) shows MinIE's annotations are more comprehensive

strengths.title: Principled multi-mode design with explicit trade-offs
strengths.description: The four minimization modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) are well-motivated and provide users with explicit control over precision-brevity trade-offs. The progression from conservative to aggressive is logical, and each mode has clear design principles (e.g., Safe mode drops only universally safe constituents).
evidence: Section 6 describes each mode with clear design rationale
Table 3 shows systematic progression in extraction length across modes
Table 4 shows corresponding precision degradation
Safe mode design (Section 6.1) is conservative and well-justified

strengths.title: Transparent acknowledgment of limitations
strengths.description: The paper explicitly acknowledges many limitations and design choices (negation scope, modality granularity, collocation handling, clause-based extraction). This transparency strengthens the paper by setting realistic expectations and identifying future work directions. Section 7.4 provides error analysis.
evidence: Lines 497-499: Explicit acknowledgment of negation scope, focus, double negation limitations
Lines 480-481: Note about more advanced modality approaches
Section 7.4: Error analysis identifying dependency parsing, collocation, NER as error sources
Lines 303-304: Explicit statement that MinIE focuses on individual clauses

strengths.title: Solid empirical evaluation with multiple datasets and baselines
strengths.description: The paper evaluates MinIE against three strong baselines (ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE) on multiple datasets (NYT-10k, NYT-200, Wiki-200). The evaluation measures multiple dimensions (precision, recall, extraction length, redundancy, annotation coverage), providing a comprehensive view of system performance.
evidence: Section 7.1 describes experimental setup with three baselines
Table 3 provides statistics on NYT-10k (10,000 sentences)
Table 4 provides precision/recall on labeled NYT and Wiki (200 sentences each)
Multiple evaluation metrics: factual precision, attribution precision, extraction length, redundancy

strengths.title: Practical system with clear implementation details
strengths.description: MinIE is implemented as a concrete system on top of ClausIE with clear algorithmic descriptions. The paper provides sufficient implementation detail (e.g., how to construct potentially stable subconstituents in Section 6.2) to enable reproduction and extension. Authors commit to releasing code and data.
evidence: Section 3 provides clear architecture overview (Figure 1)
Sections 4-6 provide detailed algorithmic descriptions
Section 6.2 provides detailed algorithm for constructing potentially stable subconstituents

concerns.title: Lack of formal definition of 'overly specific'
concerns.description: The core concept of 'overly specific' is never formally defined. The paper relies on intuitive linguistic judgment and domain-independent heuristics, but provides no formal criteria or metrics for what constitutes 'overly specific' vs. 'appropriately specific'. This makes it difficult to assess whether minimization decisions are principled or ad-hoc.

Section 6 describes minimization modes but each mode defines 'safe' or 'stable' constituents without formal criteria
No semantic equivalence metric provided to validate that minimized extractions preserve meaning
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide formal definition of 'overly specific' (e.g., constituents that do not affect core semantic role of subject/relation/object). Alternatively, define it operationally in terms of information-theoretic measures (e.g., constituents that reduce mutual information with downstream task labels below threshold).

concerns.title: Annotation scheme sufficiency not validated
concerns.description: The paper asserts that polarity, modality, attribution, and quantity annotations capture removed information without loss of meaning, but provides no formal validation. No semantic equivalence metric is used to verify that (minimized extraction + annotations) is semantically equivalent to (original extraction). This is a critical assumption that is never tested.

No inter-annotator agreement or reliability metrics reported
No evaluation of whether downstream tasks benefit from annotated minimized extractions vs. original extractions
Table 3 shows annotation coverage but not annotation correctness
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct human evaluation to verify that (minimized extraction + annotations) conveys same information as original extraction. Measure inter-annotator agreement on annotation correctness. Evaluate downstream task performance (IR, QA, KB extension) with and without annotations to validate utility.

concerns.title: Negation detection limited to 'easy cases' with low coverage
concerns.description: Negation detection uses a simple lexicon {no, not, never, none} and explicitly does not handle negation scope, focus, or double negation. Coverage is low (3.7% of extractions). The paper acknowledges these limitations but does not quantify the frequency of missed negations or their impact on downstream tasks.

Table 3: Only 3.7% of extractions have negative polarity annotation

No error analysis of false negatives or false positives in negation detection
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify frequency of missed negations in evaluation dataset. Analyze error cases (scope, focus, double negation) and estimate their frequency. Consider implementing more sophisticated negation detection (e.g., using negation scope resolution from Blanco & Moldovan 2011). Evaluate impact of missed negations on downstream task performance.

concerns.title: Modality representation uses only binary CT/PS distinction
concerns.description: Modality is represented with only two levels (Certainty vs. Possibility), whereas more nuanced approaches exist (Saurí & Pustejovsky 2012). The paper acknowledges this limitation but does not explore whether finer-grained modality distinctions would improve downstream task performance.

Table 2 shows only CT and PS modality values
No justification for why binary distinction is sufficient
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Justify choice of binary CT/PS distinction (e.g., empirical analysis showing downstream tasks do not benefit from finer-grained modality). Alternatively, extend annotation scheme to support more nuanced modality levels and evaluate impact on downstream tasks.

concerns.title: Attribution detection limited to subordinate clauses and 'according to' patterns
concerns.description: Attribution detection is limited to ccomp (clausal complement) dependency relations and 'according to' patterns. Other attribution sources (parenthetical attributions, implicit attributions, other syntactic patterns) are missed. The paper does not quantify coverage or analyze missed attribution cases.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze evaluation dataset to identify attribution sources beyond ccomp and 'according to' patterns. Implement additional patterns (e.g., parenthetical attributions, implicit attributions from context). Evaluate coverage improvement and impact on downstream tasks.

concerns.title: Redundancy definition is simplistic and may miss semantic redundancy
concerns.description: Redundancy is defined as subsequence matching: 't1 redundant if it appears as subsequence in some other triple t2'. This definition misses semantic redundancy (paraphrases, near-duplicates with different word order, synonymous relations). This may inflate recall metrics and underestimate the amount of true redundancy in the data.
evidence: Section 7.1 (lines 755-756): 'For simplicity, we consider a triple t1 redundant if it appears as subsequence in some other triple t2'
Table 3: Redundancy statistics based on this definition
No analysis of semantic redundancy (e.g., 'was born on' vs. 'was born in')
No comparison to other redundancy definitions
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Extend redundancy definition to capture semantic redundancy (e.g., using entailment or similarity metrics). Analyze how many additional redundancies are captured by semantic definition. Re-evaluate recall metrics with semantic redundancy definition. Discuss implications for comparison to baseline systems.

concerns.title: Precision evaluation on small labeled samples without statistical significance testing
concerns.description: Precision is evaluated on only 200-sentence samples (NYT, Wiki). No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported. With such small sample sizes, differences in precision may not be statistically significant. This weakens claims about superiority over baseline systems.

No discussion of statistical significance
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report confidence intervals (95%) for all precision metrics. Conduct significance tests (e.g., McNemar's test) to compare systems. Increase labeled sample size if feasible. Discuss implications of small sample size for claims about superiority.

concerns.title: Attribution precision based on sparse data with low reliability
concerns.description: Attribution precision is evaluated on data where most sentences lack attributions. Authors acknowledge 'should be taken with a grain of salt' (line 777). concerns.title: Frequency threshold for MinIE-F appears arbitrary without sensitivity analysis
concerns.description: MinIE-F uses frequency threshold ≥10 for stable constituents, but no justification or sensitivity analysis is provided. Justify choice of ≥10 based on empirical analysis. Provide guidance on how to set threshold for new domains (e.g., based on corpus size or domain characteristics).

concerns.title: Collocation dictionary may miss domain-specific collocations
concerns.description: MinIE-C uses collocations from WordNet and Wiktionary, which are domain-independent. concerns.title: Clause-based extraction may miss cross-clause relations
concerns.description: MinIE focuses on extractions from individual clauses (with exception of attribution). This may miss cross-clause relations and complex sentence structures. concerns.description: MinIE relies on ClausIE, which uses dependency parsing. Authors acknowledge 'errors in dependency parsing transfer over to errors in MinIE' (lines 801-803) and identify this as 'main source of errors in MinIE-S'. However, impact is not quantified or analyzed.

comparable_works.relevance: Direct predecessor system that MinIE builds upon
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: MinIE extends ClausIE with minimization and annotations. ClausIE focuses on clause-based extraction; MinIE adds constituent removal and annotation framework. MinIE achieves higher precision (0.79 vs 0.68) on NYT dataset.

comparable_works.relevance: Closest system in spirit to MinIE; also uses aggressive minimization
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Both use minimization but differ in approach. Stanford OIE deletes subconstituents via typed dependencies and frequency constraints. MinIE uses more principled modes (Safe/Frequency/Collocations/Aggressive) and adds annotation framework. MinIE achieves higher precision (0.79 vs 0.62) but Stanford produces shorter extractions (6.6 vs 7.2 words for MinIE-S).

comparable_works.relevance: Introduces annotated OIE extractions concept
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: OLLIE uses annotations for attribution and clause modifiers. MinIE extends this with polarity, modality, and quantity annotations. MinIE achieves higher precision (0.79 vs 0.71) on NYT dataset. OLLIE's attribution detection is limited to ccomp dependency; MinIE adds 'according to' patterns.

comparable_works.relevance: Introduces frequency-based minimization for OIE
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: ReVerb uses frequency constraints to avoid overly-specific relations. MinIE-F adopts similar approach but applies it to subjects and arguments as well. MinIE extends frequency-based approach with additional minimization modes.

comparable_works.relevance: Introduce nested/minimal facts representation
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: CSDIE and NestIE use nested representations with pointers to other extractions. MinIE uses flat representation with annotations instead. MinIE does not currently handle nested extractions (acknowledged in Conclusion).

comparable_works.relevance: Foundational work on factuality annotation and modality representation
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: MinIE adapts factuality annotation scheme (polarity + modality) from Saurí & Pustejovsky. MinIE uses simplified binary CT/PS modality; Saurí & Pustejovsky use more nuanced approach. MinIE applies factuality to OIE extractions; Saurí & Pustejovsky apply to events.

alternative_interpretations: MinIE's precision improvement over ClausIE could be attributed to implicit extractions or CoreNLP version differences rather than minimization itself. An ablation study would be needed to isolate minimization contribution.

The low coverage of negative polarity annotations (3.7%) could indicate either that negations are rare in text or that negation detection is limited. Without error analysis, it's unclear which interpretation is correct.

The modest precision difference between MinIE-F and MinIE-C (0.78 vs 0.78) could suggest that dictionary choice is not critical, or it could indicate that both dictionaries are similarly incomplete. More analysis is needed.

The claim that MinIE consolidates redundant extractions could be reinterpreted as MinIE simply producing fewer total extractions (45,649 vs 58,420 for ClausIE), not necessarily consolidating redundancies. The paper does not verify that minimization actually consolidates ClausIE redundancies.

The 'critical gap' of negative evidence in prior OIE systems is asserted but not empirically demonstrated. It's unclear whether prior systems actually fail to represent negations or simply represent them differently.

The paper's claim that minimized extractions are more useful for downstream tasks is not validated. It's possible that original extractions are equally or more useful for some tasks (e.g., tasks requiring fine-grained information).

confidence_interval.rationale: MinIE is a well-executed methodological contribution with solid engineering, clear presentation, and comprehensive evaluation. The paper's strengths (well-motivated problem, comprehensive annotation framework, multi-mode design, transparent acknowledgment of limitations) outweigh its weaknesses (limited conceptual novelty, unvalidated downstream utility, small evaluation samples, simplistic redundancy definition). The main sources of uncertainty are: (1) whether downstream task evaluation would validate practical utility, (2) whether the annotation scheme is sufficiently expressive for downstream tasks, (3) whether the contribution is sufficiently novel for a top-tier venue. The paper is likely to be accepted at a good conference but may not be accepted at a top-tier venue without downstream task evaluation or stronger novelty claims. specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: MinIE is a methodologically sound engineering contribution that addresses a real problem in OIE: overly-specific extractions that obscure semantic equivalence. The system design is principled, separating minimization from annotation, and the four-mode architecture enables tunable trade-offs. However, the paper exhibits several methodological gaps that limit confidence in its claims: (1) evaluation is limited to small labeled samples (200 sentences) without statistical significance testing; (2) core assumptions about negation, modality, and attribution detection are acknowledged as handling only 'easy cases' but impact is not quantified; (3) the redundancy definition is simplistic (subsequence matching) and may not capture semantic redundancy; (4) no downstream task evaluation validates that minimized extractions improve utility for IR, QA, or KB extension; (5) dependency parsing errors propagate through the pipeline but their frequency and impact are not measured. The paper makes incremental contributions over prior work (particularly Stanford OIE and OLLIE) but the novelty is primarily in the annotation framework and multi-mode design rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation. Strengths include explicit handling of linguistic phenomena, transparent acknowledgment of limitations, and reproducibility commitment. The work is technically competent but would benefit from larger-scale evaluation, statistical rigor, and downstream task validation.

concerns.title: Evaluation on small labeled samples without statistical significance testing
concerns.description: Precision and recall are evaluated on only 200-sentence samples (NYT, Wiki). No confidence intervals, p-values, or statistical significance tests are reported. This makes it impossible to assess whether observed differences (e.g., 0.79 vs 0.68) are statistically meaningful or due to sampling variance.

No discussion of sample size adequacy or power analysis
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct statistical significance testing (e.g., bootstrap confidence intervals, permutation tests) on precision/recall differences. Report 95% confidence intervals for all metrics. Perform power analysis to justify sample size. Consider larger labeled datasets if feasible.

concerns.title: Negation detection limited to 'easy cases' with unquantified impact
concerns.description: Negation detection uses a simple lexicon {no, not, never, none} and explicitly does not handle negation scope, focus, or double negation. Authors acknowledge this limitation but do not quantify how often these cases occur in the evaluation datasets or how many negations are missed.

concerns.description: Redundancy is defined as subsequence matching: 't1 redundant if it appears as subsequence in some other triple t2'. This misses semantic redundancy (paraphrases, synonymous relations, near-duplicates). The claim that MinIE consolidates redundancy is not independently verified.

Compare redundancy rates before and after minimization to isolate MinIE's contribution. Analyze whether consolidation actually occurs or if it merely reveals pre-existing redundancy.

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Both systems minimize extractions, but Stanford OIE uses typed dependencies for minimization while MinIE uses principled modes. MinIE adds annotations for polarity, modality, attribution, quantities. Stanford OIE produces more redundant extractions.

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Both use annotations, but OLLIE only annotates attribution and clause modifiers. MinIE extends annotation scheme to include polarity, modality, quantities. MinIE achieves higher precision (0.79 vs 0.71 on NYT).

comparable_works.relevance: Foundation system on which MinIE is built
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: MinIE uses ClausIE as underlying extractor and adds minimization and annotation layers. MinIE achieves higher precision (0.79 vs 0.68 on NYT) and shorter extractions (7.2 vs 10.9 words).

comparable_works.relevance: Early OIE system that introduced frequency-based minimization
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: ReVerb uses frequency constraints to avoid overly-specific relations. MinIE-F extends this idea to subjects and arguments. MinIE's approach is more principled with multiple modes.

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: CSDIE and NestIE use nested representations with pointers to other extractions. MinIE uses flat representations with annotations. MinIE does not currently handle nested extractions.

The low negative polarity coverage (3.7%) may indicate that negation is rare in the evaluation datasets rather than that MinIE's detection is limited. Without negation frequency analysis, this is unclear.

The claim that MinIE consolidates redundancy may be misleading. MinIE may simply produce fewer extractions overall (45,649 vs 58,420 for ClausIE), which could be due to different extraction strategies rather than consolidation.
The 'critical gap' of negative evidence in prior systems may be overstated. If negation is rare in real-world text, the practical impact of missing negative polarity annotations may be limited.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: MinIE combines existing ideas (minimization from Stanford OIE, annotations from OLLIE, frequency constraints from ReVerb) in a principled way. The contribution is primarily engineering-driven (multi-mode design, richer annotation framework) rather than conceptually novel. This is appropriate for a methodological contribution but limits the innovation signal.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If downstream task evaluation (IR, QA, KB extension) showed that minimized extractions with annotations improve performance, the contribution would be more compelling.
If statistical significance testing showed that precision improvements are robust and not due to sampling variance, the empirical claims would be stronger.
If the paper quantified the impact of unhandled linguistic phenomena (negation scope, modality nuance, attribution patterns), the scope boundaries would be clearer and more credible.
If the paper provided guidance on mode selection for different applications, the multi-mode design would be more practical.
If the paper demonstrated that negative polarity annotations improve downstream reasoning tasks, the claim about addressing a 'critical gap' would be validated.

confidence_interval.rationale: MinIE is a technically sound methodological contribution with clear practical value (shorter extractions, competitive precision, richer annotations). However, significant methodological gaps limit confidence: (1) small labeled samples without statistical significance testing; (2) unquantified impact of acknowledged limitations (negation scope, modality simplification); (3) no downstream task evaluation; (4) incremental novelty over Stanford OIE and OLLIE. The paper would be strengthened by larger-scale evaluation, statistical rigor, and downstream task validation. The work is suitable for publication at a venue focused on methodological contributions (e.g., ACL, EMNLP) but would benefit from addressing the major methodological concerns before acceptance at a top-tier venue.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: MinIE represents a well-motivated incremental refinement of the OIE paradigm, building directly on ClausIE while introducing systematic minimization and structured annotation. The contribution is engineering-driven and principled, addressing a genuine problem (overly-specific extractions) through a multi-mode design that trades off brevity against precision. The novelty is primarily in the *combination* of techniques (minimization + annotation framework) and the explicit handling of linguistic phenomena (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) as separable concerns. However, the individual techniques are largely domain-adaptations of existing ideas: negation detection via lexicon (simple, acknowledged as limited), modality via modal verbs (standard), attribution via subordinate clauses (OLLIE precedent), and frequency-based minimization (ReVerb precedent). The annotation scheme itself is incremental over OLLIE, adding factuality and quantity annotations. The core novelty claim—that negative polarity annotations address a critical gap—is empirically weak: only 3.7% of extractions receive negative polarity, and the paper provides no downstream validation that this addresses the stated reasoning problem. The multi-mode design is pragmatic but not theoretically novel; it is a tuning mechanism rather than a conceptual advance. Strengths lie in systematic engineering, comprehensive evaluation on multiple datasets, and practical utility. Concerns center on limited scope of minimization techniques, weak validation of key claims, and absence of downstream task evaluation.

strengths.title: Principled multi-mode design with clear trade-offs
strengths.description: The four minimization modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) provide a pragmatic framework for balancing brevity against precision. Each mode is clearly motivated and documented, allowing users to select based on downstream task requirements. This is a well-engineered solution to the inherent tension in minimization.

Table 3 and Table 4 demonstrate empirical trade-offs across modes
Safe mode explicitly restricts to 'universally safe' operations, reducing risk of over-minimization

strengths.title: Comprehensive annotation framework for linguistic phenomena
strengths.description: MinIE introduces a structured annotation scheme that separates polarity, modality, attribution, and quantity information from the extraction itself. This is more expressive than prior work (OLLIE) and addresses multiple linguistic dimensions systematically. The annotation scheme is domain-independent and reusable.

Table 1 and Table 2 show examples of annotations preserving information
Table 3 shows annotation coverage across large dataset (NYT-10k)
Annotations include both factuality (polarity/modality) and metadata (original relation, argument)

strengths.title: Empirical evaluation on multiple datasets with consistent improvements
strengths.description: The paper evaluates MinIE on three datasets (NYT-10k, NYT-200, Wiki-200) using multiple metrics (precision, recall, extraction length, redundancy). MinIE-S consistently achieves higher precision than ClausIE while producing shorter extractions, demonstrating practical utility.

Table 4: MinIE-S precision 0.79-0.83 vs ClausIE 0.68-0.73 across datasets

strengths.title: Explicit acknowledgment of limitations and scope boundaries
strengths.description: The authors are transparent about the limitations of their approach. They explicitly state that negation detection is restricted to 'easy cases' (Section 5.1), modality uses only binary CT/PS distinction (Section 5.2), and clause-based extraction may miss cross-clause relations (Section 3). This honesty about scope is valuable.
