strengths.title: Systematic handling of linguistic phenomena through constituent removal
strengths.description: The paper provides a principled approach to identifying and removing overly-specific constituents while preserving semantic information through annotations. The enrichment of relations (Section 4.1) and basic minimization (Section 5) are well-motivated.
evidence: Section 4.1 describes relation enrichment based on clause types (SV, SVA, SVC, SVO, SVOO, SVOA, SVOC), making relations more informative
Section 5 systematically addresses polarity, modality, attribution, and quantities with corresponding removal and annotation strategies
Table 1 demonstrates the approach on a complex example, showing how different constituents are removed and annotated

concerns.title: Lack of formal definition of 'overly specific'
concerns.description: The paper relies on intuitive linguistic judgment to define 'overly specific' constituents but provides no formal definition or semantic equivalence metric. This makes the core concept of the paper imprecise and difficult to generalize.
evidence: Introduction: 'A key challenge in OIE is to avoid overly-specific extractions' (line 045-046) but no formal definition provided
Table 1 shows examples of overly-specific extractions but the criteria for identifying them are implicit
Section 6 describes minimization modes but the decision of what is 'overly specific' is based on heuristics (e.g., 'universally safe' in MinIE-S, frequency threshold in MinIE-F)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a formal definition of 'overly specific' based on semantic equivalence or information-theoretic measures. Alternatively, define it operationally in terms of the minimization modes and provide empirical validation that removed constituents do not affect downstream task performance.

concerns.title: Annotation scheme sufficiency not validated
concerns.description: The paper asserts that annotations preserve meaning of removed constituents but does not formally validate that the annotation scheme is sufficient to capture all removed information or that downstream tasks can recover original meaning from annotations.
evidence: Abstract: 'To retain the original meaning to the extent possible, MinIE provides suitable annotations for each extraction' (line 018-019) but 'to the extent possible' is vague
Section 5 describes annotation types but no evaluation of annotation completeness or correctness
No downstream task evaluation (IR, QA, KB extension) to validate that annotations enable recovery of original meaning
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct downstream task evaluation (e.g., IR, QA, KB extension) comparing minimized extractions with annotations to original extractions. Alternatively, conduct human evaluation of whether annotations preserve meaning of removed constituents.

concerns.title: Negation detection limited to 'easy cases' with low coverage
concerns.description: Negation detection is limited to relation-level negations via a simple lexicon {no, not, never, none}. The paper acknowledges that negation scope, focus, and double negation are not handled. Coverage is low (3.7%), raising questions about whether this represents true negation frequency or detection limitations.
evidence: Section 5.1: 'MinIE does not address these problems, but restricts attention to the easy cases' (line 499-500)
Table 3: Only 3.7% of extractions have negative polarity annotation
Section 5.1: 'if a negations occurs in the subject or argument of the extraction, MinIE misses it' (line 489-490)
Example: 'No people were hurt in the fire' is handled via quantity annotation, not negation annotation (line 490-492)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify the frequency of unhandled negation cases (scope, focus, double negation) in the evaluation datasets. Provide error analysis showing false negatives from negation detection. Consider implementing more sophisticated negation detection (e.g., using negation scope resolution techniques).

concerns.title: Modality representation limited to binary CT/PS distinction
concerns.description: Modality is represented using only two levels (Certainty and Possibility), whereas more nuanced approaches exist (Saurí & Pustejovsky 2012). Information loss from this simplification is not analyzed.
evidence: Section 5.2: 'MinIE's approach focuses on the easy cases and uses only the CT and PS levels. A more advanced approach is taken by (Saurí and Pustejovsky, 2012)' (line 479-480)
Table 2 shows only CT and PS modality values; no intermediate levels
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze information loss from binary modality representation. Compare MinIE's CT/PS approach to Saurí & Pustejovsky's more nuanced approach on downstream tasks to quantify the impact of simplification.

concerns.title: Attribution detection limited to subordinate clauses and 'according to' patterns
concerns.description: Attribution detection is limited to two patterns: subordinate clauses and 'according to' adverbials. Other attribution sources (parenthetical attributions, implicit attributions, etc.) are not detected. Completeness of attribution detection is not evaluated.
evidence: Section 5.3: 'We extract attributions from subordinate clauses as well as from an "according to" pattern' (line 523-524)
Section 5.3: 'MinIE searches for extractions that contain entire clauses as arguments' (line 525-526)
No evaluation of attribution detection completeness; only coverage statistics provided (10.7% in Table 3)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze missed attribution cases in the evaluation datasets. Identify other attribution patterns (parenthetical, implicit, etc.) and extend attribution detection to cover them. Evaluate attribution detection precision and recall separately.

concerns.title: Simplistic redundancy definition may not capture semantic redundancy
concerns.description: Redundancy is defined as subsequence matching ('t1 redundant if it appears as subsequence in some other triple t2'). This definition may miss semantic redundancy (paraphrases, near-duplicates) and could misrepresent recall metrics.
evidence: Section 7.1: 'For simplicity, we consider a triple t1 redundant if it appears as subsequence in some other triple t2 produced by the same extractor from the same sentence' (line 755-756)
Table 3 shows redundancy statistics but no analysis of semantic redundancy
Example in Table 1: extraction 5 is redundant given extraction 6 (line 756-757), but this is based on subsequence matching
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Extend redundancy definition to capture semantic redundancy (paraphrases, near-duplicates). Conduct manual analysis of redundant extractions to identify semantic redundancy not captured by subsequence matching. Re-evaluate recall metrics using semantic redundancy definition.

concerns.title: Precision evaluation on small labeled samples without statistical significance testing
concerns.description: Precision is evaluated on small labeled samples (200 sentences each for NYT and Wiki). No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are provided. Differences between systems may not be statistically significant.
evidence: Section 7.1: 'We used as datasets (1) a random sample of 10,000 sentences from the New York Times Annotated Corpus (NYT-10k), (2) a random sample of 200 sentences from the same corpus (NYT), and (3) a random sample of 200 sentences from Wikipedia (Wiki)' (line 705-708)
Table 4 shows precision results on NYT and Wiki but no confidence intervals or significance tests
Precision differences between MinIE-S, MinIE-F, MinIE-C are small (0.79, 0.78, 0.78 on NYT) but statistical significance not tested
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct statistical significance testing (e.g., chi-square test, bootstrap confidence intervals) on precision differences. Report confidence intervals for all precision estimates. Consider increasing labeled sample size or using cross-validation to improve statistical power.

concerns.title: Attribution precision based on sparse data with unclear reliability
concerns.description: Attribution precision is evaluated on a small subset of sentences containing attributions. Authors acknowledge 'these numbers should be taken with a grain of salt' (line 789), but the reliability and generalizability of attribution precision estimates are unclear.
evidence: Section 7.3: 'As for attribution precision, most of the sentences in our samples did not contain attributions; these numbers should thus be taken with a grain of salt' (line 788-789)
Table 4 shows attribution precision (0.94, 0.93, etc.) but sample sizes are not reported
No analysis of how many sentences contain attributions or how many attribution instances are evaluated
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report sample sizes for attribution precision evaluation. Conduct separate evaluation on sentences with attributions to provide more reliable estimates. Consider using a dataset with higher attribution density or manually annotating more attribution instances.

concerns.title: Frequency threshold for MinIE-F appears arbitrary without sensitivity analysis
concerns.description: MinIE-F uses a frequency threshold of ≥10 for including constituents in dictionary D. This threshold appears arbitrary and no sensitivity analysis is provided to justify the choice or explore its impact.
evidence: Section 6.2: 'we additionally include all frequent (e.g., frequency ≥ 10) subjects, relations, and arguments into D' (line 587-588)
No justification provided for the choice of threshold ≥10
No sensitivity analysis exploring different threshold values
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct sensitivity analysis on the frequency threshold, evaluating precision and recall for different threshold values (e.g., ≥5, ≥10, ≥20). Provide justification for the chosen threshold based on empirical results.

concerns.title: Collocation dictionary may miss domain-specific collocations
concerns.description: MinIE-C uses collocations from WordNet and Wiktionary, which are domain-independent. Domain-specific collocations are missed, leading to incorrect minimization (e.g., 'assistant director' broken into 'director'). Error frequency is not quantified.
evidence: Section 6.2: 'we included all multi-word expressions from WordNet and Wiktionary, which we consider domain-independent' (line 580-581)

Section 7.4: 'we sometimes drop adjectives which in fact form collocations (e.g., "assistant director") with the noun they are modifying, but the collocation is not present in the dictionary' (line 809-811)
No quantification of collocation handling errors
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify the frequency of collocation handling errors in the evaluation datasets. Analyze which types of collocations are missed (e.g., domain-specific, rare collocations). Propose methods to automatically extract domain-specific collocations from text corpora.

concerns.title: No downstream task evaluation validating utility of minimized extractions
concerns.description: The paper does not evaluate whether minimized extractions with annotations improve performance on downstream tasks (IR, QA, KB extension). Utility of minimization for downstream applications is not demonstrated.
evidence: Introduction: 'The extractions of OIE systems are useful for tasks such as information retrieval (Löser et al., 2012), question answering (Fader et al., 2014), knowledge-base extension (Dong et al., 2014; Riedel et al., 2013; Petroni et al., 2015)' (line 010-013)
No downstream task evaluation in Section 7
No comparison of downstream task performance using MinIE extractions vs. baseline extractions
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct downstream task evaluation on IR, QA, or KB extension tasks. Compare performance using MinIE extractions (with annotations) to baseline extractions. Demonstrate that minimization and annotations improve downstream task performance.

concerns.title: Comparison to Stanford OIE complicated by redundant extraction generation
concerns.description: Stanford OIE produces many redundant extraction variants by dropping different subsets of words. When redundancy is discounted, the comparison becomes less clear. Fairness of comparison is questionable.
evidence: Section 7.2: 'Stanford OIE produces many extraction variants by dropping different subsets of words' (line 721-722)
Table 3: Stanford OIE produces 43,365 total extractions but only 16,779 non-redundant (61% redundancy)
Section 7.3: 'Surprisingly to us, even MinIE's aggressive mode achieved higher precision than Stanford OIE' (line 783-784)
Authors note that Stanford OIE's short extraction length is due to 'aggressive creation of (shorter) redundant extractions' (line 722-723)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct separate evaluation comparing MinIE to Stanford OIE using only non-redundant extractions. Discuss fairness of comparison given Stanford OIE's redundant extraction generation strategy. Consider whether Stanford OIE's approach is fundamentally different from MinIE's.

concerns.title: Extraction length as proxy for minimality not validated
concerns.description: The paper uses mean word count as a proxy for minimality but does not validate that word count correlates with semantic minimality. Shorter extractions may retain redundant information; longer extractions may be more informative.
evidence: Section 7.1: 'we use these numbers as a proxy for minimality' (line 751-752)
Table 3 shows extraction length statistics but no validation that word count correlates with semantic minimality
No analysis of whether shorter extractions are actually more minimal in semantic terms
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate that word count correlates with semantic minimality. Conduct manual evaluation of whether shorter extractions are actually more minimal. Consider alternative minimality metrics (e.g., information content, semantic redundancy).

concerns.title: Dependency parsing errors propagate through pipeline with unquantified impact

comparable_works.relevance: Direct predecessor system; MinIE is built on top of ClausIE
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: ClausIE performs clause-based extraction without minimization or annotations. MinIE adds minimization and annotation layers on top of ClausIE's extractions. MinIE-S achieves higher precision (0.79 vs 0.68) but produces fewer total extractions.

comparable_works.relevance: Closest system in spirit; also uses aggressive minimization
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Stanford OIE uses aggressive minimization by deleting subconstituents connected by typed dependencies. MinIE differs by separating polarity/modality/attribution/quantities and using multiple modes. MinIE-S achieves higher precision (0.79 vs 0.62 on NYT) but Stanford OIE produces shorter extractions due to redundant variants.

comparable_works.relevance: Introduces annotated OIE extractions; MinIE extends this approach
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: OLLIE uses annotations for attribution and clausal modifiers. MinIE extends with factuality (polarity/modality) and quantity annotations. MinIE-S achieves higher precision (0.79 vs 0.71 on NYT) and produces shorter extractions (7.2±4.2 vs 9.3±5.2).

comparable_works.relevance: Introduces frequency-based minimization for relations
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: ReVerb uses frequency constraints to avoid overly-specific relations. MinIE-F extends this approach to subjects and arguments. MinIE also adds annotation framework not present in ReVerb.

comparable_works.relevance: Introduces factuality representation with polarity and modality
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Saurí & Pustejovsky use more nuanced modality levels (not just CT/PS). MinIE adopts their factuality framework but simplifies modality to binary distinction. MinIE applies factuality representation to OIE extractions.

comparable_works.relevance: Introduce nested/minimal facts representation
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: CSDIE and NestIE use nested representations with pointers to other extractions. MinIE uses flat representations with annotations instead. MinIE does not currently handle nested extractions.

alternative_interpretations: The low negative polarity coverage (3.7%) may indicate that negation detection is limited rather than that negations are rare in text. The claim that MinIE addresses a 'critical gap' in negative evidence may be overstated if most negations are not detected.

The precision improvements of MinIE-S over ClausIE may be due to factors other than minimization: implicit extractions, breaking up long error-prone extractions, and using a different version of Stanford CoreNLP. The contribution of minimization itself is unclear.

The redundancy consolidation claim may reflect pre-existing redundancy in ClausIE output rather than consolidation caused by minimization. Minimization may simply reveal redundancy rather than cause it.

The trade-off between extraction brevity and precision may not be as favorable as claimed. The precision drop from MinIE-S (0.79) to MinIE-A (0.68) is substantial (11 percentage points), and the extraction length reduction is modest (7.2 to 4.7 words, 35% reduction).

The annotation framework may not be sufficient to preserve meaning of removed constituents. Downstream tasks may require access to original constituents rather than annotations to achieve good performance.

The simplistic redundancy definition (subsequence matching) may overestimate recall improvements. Semantic redundancy (paraphrases, near-duplicates) may not be captured, leading to misleading recall metrics.

The frequency threshold (≥10) for MinIE-F may be too low, leading to over-minimization and information loss. Alternatively, it may be too high, leading to under-minimization and overly-specific extractions.
The collocation dictionary (WordNet + Wiktionary) may be insufficient for domain-specific applications. Domain-specific collocations may be missed, leading to incorrect minimization.

The clause-based extraction approach may be fundamentally limited for complex sentences with cross-clause relations. Extending MinIE to handle cross-clause relations may require significant architectural changes.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: MinIE combines existing techniques (clause-based extraction, lexicon-based negation detection, frequency-based minimization, annotation-based representation) into a multi-mode system. The novelty is primarily in the combination and systematic application rather than in fundamentally new conceptual frames. The annotation framework is novel for OIE (particularly negative polarity representation), but individual minimization techniques are largely domain-adaptations of prior work (ReVerb, Stanford OIE, OLLIE). The contribution is engineering-driven and incremental rather than conceptually disruptive.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If downstream task evaluation (IR, QA, KB extension) demonstrated that minimized extractions with annotations improve performance compared to baseline extractions, the contribution would be significantly strengthened.

If formal validation of meaning preservation (e.g., semantic equivalence metrics, entailment-based evaluation) demonstrated that annotations capture all removed information, the core claim would be more credible.
If negation detection were extended to handle scope, focus, and double negation with higher coverage (>10%), the negative polarity claim would be more compelling.
If statistical significance testing on precision differences demonstrated that improvements are significant (not due to random variation), the empirical claims would be stronger.
If the paper provided formal definitions of 'overly specific' and 'minimality' based on semantic or information-theoretic measures, the conceptual foundation would be more rigorous.
If the paper demonstrated that minimization actually consolidates redundant extractions (rather than merely revealing pre-existing redundancy), the redundancy consolidation claim would be validated.
If the paper evaluated performance on complex multi-clause sentences and demonstrated that clause-based extraction is sufficient, the scope limitations would be less concerning.

novelty_lenses.verdict: Incremental refinement of OIE paradigm with engineering-driven improvements
novelty_lenses.rationale: MinIE represents a well-motivated incremental refinement of the OIE paradigm, building directly on ClausIE while introducing systematic minimization and structured annotation. The novelty is primarily in the combination of techniques (minimization + annotation framework) and the explicit handling of linguistic phenomena (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) as separable concerns. However, individual techniques are largely domain-adaptations of existing ideas: negation detection via lexicon (simple, acknowledged as limited), modality via modal verbs (standard), attribution via subordinate clauses (OLLIE precedent), frequency-based minimization (ReVerb precedent). The annotation scheme itself is incremental over OLLIE, adding factuality and quantity annotations. The core novelty claim—that negative polarity annotations address a critical gap—is empirically weak: only 3.7% of extractions receive negative polarity, and the paper provides no downstream validation.

novelty_lenses.verdict: Engineering-driven methodological contribution that is fundamentally incremental rather than disruptive
novelty_lenses.rationale: MinIE presents an engineering-driven methodological contribution that combines incremental improvements over prior systems (ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE) with a novel annotation-based representation framework. The core conceptual innovation—separating minimization from semantic preservation through structured annotations—is coherent and addresses a genuine gap in prior OIE work, particularly regarding negative polarity representation. However, the contribution is fundamentally incremental rather than disruptive: it combines existing techniques (clause-based extraction, lexicon-based negation detection, frequency-based minimization) into a multi-mode system with tunable aggressiveness. The novelty lies in the combination and systematic application of these techniques, not in fundamentally new conceptual frames. The annotation scheme itself, while more comprehensive than OLLIE's, draws directly from Saurí & Pustejovsky (2012) factuality representation. The paper's strength is engineering coherence and empirical validation; its limitation is conceptual incrementalism masked by comprehensive system design.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper presents a methodologically sound engineering contribution with solid empirical evaluation on labeled datasets. The main claims (minimization preserves meaning through annotations, multiple modes enable trade-offs, competitive performance with shorter extractions) are supported by evidence, though with important caveats regarding scope, formalization, and validation. The lower bound (0.65) reflects concerns about: (1) lack of formal definitions and semantic validation of core claims; (2) limited scope of linguistic phenomenon detection (acknowledged 'easy cases' only); (3) small labeled sample sizes without statistical significance testing; (4) absence of downstream task evaluation; (5) weak validation of the negative polarity claim as addressing a 'critical gap'. The upper bound (0.85) reflects strengths: (1) transparent acknowledgment of limitations; (2) comprehensive annotation framework novel for OIE; (3) principled multi-mode design with explicit trade-offs; (4) empirical evaluation on multiple datasets with consistent improvements in extraction length; (5) reproducibility commitment with code and data release. The confidence interval reflects moderate-to-high confidence in the paper's technical soundness and empirical claims, tempered by concerns about generalizability, statistical rigor, and downstream utility.

consensus_findings: MinIE addresses a genuine problem in OIE: overly-specific extractions that obscure semantic equivalence and complicate downstream tasks. The motivating example (Table 1) effectively demonstrates this problem across multiple systems.

The annotation framework (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) is comprehensive and extends prior work (OLLIE). Negative polarity representation is novel for OIE systems, though coverage is low (3.7%).
The multi-mode architecture (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) is well-motivated and principled, enabling users to select trade-offs between extraction brevity and precision.

Empirical evaluation on multiple datasets (NYT-10k, NYT, Wiki) shows consistent improvements in extraction length (7.2±4.2 to 4.7±1.9 words) and competitive precision (MinIE-S 0.79 vs ClausIE 0.68 on NYT).

The paper demonstrates intellectual honesty by explicitly acknowledging limitations: negation detection restricted to 'easy cases', modality uses binary CT/PS distinction, attribution detection limited to subordinate clauses and 'according to' patterns, clause-based extraction may miss cross-clause relations.

Individual minimization techniques are largely domain-adaptations of existing ideas (lexicon-based negation detection, frequency-based minimization from ReVerb, clause-based extraction from ClausIE, factuality representation from Saurí & Pustejovsky 2012). Novelty is primarily in the combination and systematic application.

The paper lacks downstream task evaluation validating that minimized extractions with annotations improve performance on IR, QA, or KB extension tasks. Practical utility is asserted but not demonstrated.
disagreements: Reviewers differ on the significance of the negative polarity contribution. Structure analyst and methodology auditor view it as addressing a documented gap; novelty assessors view the claim as overstated given low coverage (3.7%) and lack of downstream validation. Claim verifier notes the representation is adapted from Saurí & Pustejovsky (2012), making the novelty primarily in application scope rather than conceptual innovation.

Reviewers differ on whether the precision improvement of MinIE-S over ClausIE (0.79 vs 0.68) is attributable to minimization or confounding factors. Methodology auditor and claim verifier note that authors acknowledge 'additional high-precision implicit extractions, breaks up very long and thus error-prone extractions, and uses a different version of Stanford CoreNLP' (line 773-776), making the minimization contribution unclear. Structure analyst treats the improvement as evidence of effectiveness.

Reviewers differ on the novelty assessment. Incremental novelty lens (reviewer_3) views MinIE as a well-executed incremental refinement; disruptive novelty lens (reviewer_4) views it as fundamentally incremental rather than disruptive. Claim verifier notes the distinction is subjective and depends on evaluation criteria.

Reviewers differ on the severity of the simplistic redundancy definition (subsequence matching). Methodology auditor and claim verifier view it as a major methodological flaw that may misrepresent recall metrics; structure analyst treats it as a limitation but not a fundamental flaw.

Reviewers differ on the importance of statistical significance testing. Methodology auditor emphasizes the lack of significance tests on small samples (200 sentences) as a major methodological flaw; structure analyst notes this is common practice in OIE research due to annotation costs; claim verifier treats it as a moderate concern requiring confidence intervals.
uncertainty_hotspots: Meaning preservation claim: The paper asserts that annotations preserve meaning of removed constituents but provides no formal validation. No semantic equivalence metrics, entailment-based evaluation, or downstream task validation is provided. Reviewers agree this is a critical assumption that is never tested.

Negation detection scope and impact: The paper explicitly limits negation detection to 'easy cases' (relation-level negations via lexicon {no, not, never, none}) and acknowledges that negation scope, focus, and double negation are not handled. However, the frequency of missed negations and their impact on downstream tasks is not quantified. Reviewers agree this is a significant limitation but disagree on its severity.

Negative polarity claim as addressing 'critical gap': The paper claims negative polarity annotations address a critical gap in prior OIE systems, but evidence is weak: only 3.7% of extractions receive negative polarity, no empirical demonstration that prior systems lack negative evidence, and no downstream validation. Reviewers agree the claim is overstated but disagree on whether this is a major or minor concern.

Statistical significance of precision improvements: Precision is evaluated on small labeled samples (200 sentences each) without statistical significance testing or confidence intervals. Reviewers agree this is a methodological concern but disagree on severity: methodology auditor views it as major, structure analyst notes it is common practice, claim verifier treats it as moderate.

Redundancy definition and recall metrics: Redundancy is defined as subsequence matching, which may miss semantic redundancy (paraphrases, near-duplicates). Reviewers agree this is a limitation but disagree on impact: methodology auditor views it as major, structure analyst treats it as a limitation, claim verifier notes it may be appropriate for OIE.

Downstream task utility: The paper motivates the work with downstream tasks (IR, QA, KB extension) but does not evaluate on these tasks. Reviewers unanimously agree this is a major gap, but disagree on whether it is a fatal flaw or a limitation for future work.

Novelty assessment: Reviewers differ on whether MinIE's contribution is sufficiently novel. Incremental novelty lens views it as a well-executed refinement; disruptive novelty lens views it as fundamentally incremental. Claim verifier notes the distinction is subjective.

Precision improvement attribution: MinIE-S achieves higher precision than ClausIE (0.79 vs 0.68), but authors acknowledge this may be due to implicit extractions, breaking up long extractions, and different CoreNLP version. Reviewers agree the minimization contribution is unclear but disagree on whether this is a major concern.

Model diversity reveals a consistent pattern: all reviewers acknowledge the paper's engineering quality and empirical validation, but differ on the significance of limitations and the novelty of the contribution. The disagreements are primarily about severity assessment and novelty evaluation rather than factual disputes.
meta_review.editor_guidance: MinIE presents a methodologically sound engineering contribution to OIE that systematically addresses extraction minimization through constituent removal and annotation-based representation. The paper's core claims are largely supported by evidence, though with important caveats regarding scope, formalization, and validation. The primary decision points for the editor are: (1) Whether the engineering contribution (multi-mode design, comprehensive annotation framework) is sufficiently novel and impactful for the target venue; (2) Whether the methodological limitations (small labeled samples without statistical significance testing, absence of downstream task evaluation, simplistic redundancy definition) are acceptable or require major revisions; (3) Whether the overstated claims (particularly regarding negative polarity as addressing a 'critical gap') should be toned down or require additional evidence. The paper is suitable for publication at a venue focused on methodological contributions (e.g., ACL, EMNLP) but would benefit from addressing the major methodological concerns before acceptance at a top-tier venue. Recommended actions: (1) Conduct downstream task evaluation on at least one task (IR, QA, KB extension) to validate practical utility; (2) Report confidence intervals and statistical significance tests on precision differences; (3) Revise negative polarity claim to be more modest ('MinIE provides negative polarity annotations for relation-level negations' rather than claiming to address a 'critical gap'); (4) Provide error analysis quantifying the impact of acknowledged limitations (negation scope, modality simplification, attribution patterns, collocation handling). The paper's transparency about limitations is a significant strength that should be preserved.
meta_review.author_guidance: The paper makes solid contributions to OIE but would be strengthened by addressing the following concerns: (1) Downstream task evaluation: Evaluate MinIE on information retrieval, question answering, or knowledge base extension tasks. Compare performance using minimized extractions with annotations to baseline extractions. This would validate the practical utility of your approach and strengthen the motivation. (2) Statistical rigor: Report 95% confidence intervals for all precision estimates. Conduct statistical significance tests (e.g., McNemar's test) to compare systems. Consider increasing labeled sample size or using cross-validation to improve statistical power. (3) Negation detection: Quantify the frequency of unhandled negation cases (scope, focus, double negation) in your evaluation datasets. Provide error analysis showing false negatives from negation detection. Consider implementing more sophisticated negation detection (e.g., using negation scope resolution techniques). (4) Redundancy analysis: Extend redundancy definition to capture semantic redundancy (paraphrases, near-duplicates). Conduct manual analysis of redundant extractions to identify semantic redundancy not captured by subsequence matching. Re-evaluate recall metrics using semantic redundancy definition. (5) Meaning preservation: Conduct human evaluation to verify that (minimized extraction + annotations) conveys the same information as original extraction. Measure inter-annotator agreement on annotation correctness. (6) Revise claims: Tone down the claim about negative polarity addressing a 'critical gap' to be more modest. Provide empirical evidence that prior OIE systems cannot represent negations or conduct downstream task evaluation validating that negative polarity annotations improve performance. (7) Sensitivity analysis: Conduct sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters (frequency threshold for MinIE-F, collocation dictionary sources, negation lexicon). Provide guidance on parameter selection for different applications. (8) Error analysis: Quantify the frequency of dependency parsing errors, collocation handling errors, and NER failures in your evaluation datasets. Analyze the impact of each error source on MinIE precision. (9) Annotation validation: Report inter-annotator agreement metrics for the annotation scheme. Evaluate annotation correctness, not just coverage. (10) Clarify novelty: Explicitly clarify which contributions are novel vs. incremental. Emphasize the combination of techniques and the systematic application of minimization across multiple linguistic phenomena.
transparency_report: The paper is generally transparent about limitations. Authors explicitly acknowledge that negation detection is restricted to 'easy cases' and that more advanced approaches exist (Section 5.1, line 497-500).
The paper provides clear descriptions of the minimization modes and their trade-offs, allowing readers to understand the design choices (Section 6).
The paper includes error analysis (Section 7.4) identifying dependency parsing, collocation handling, and NER as error sources.
However, the paper does not provide statistical significance testing for precision comparisons, making it difficult to assess whether observed differences are meaningful.
The paper does not provide downstream task evaluation, leaving open the question of whether the minimization and annotation choices actually improve downstream task performance.
The paper does not quantify the impact of dependency parsing errors, collocation handling errors, or NER errors, making it difficult to assess the relative importance of different error sources.
The paper does not provide inter-annotator agreement metrics for the annotation scheme, making it unclear how reliable the annotations are.
The paper does not provide sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters (frequency threshold, collocation dictionary, negation lexicon), making it unclear how robust the approach is to these choices.
The paper acknowledges that attribution precision estimates are unreliable due to sparse data ('should be taken with a grain of salt'), appropriately flagging unreliable metrics.

The paper notes that MinIE-S precision improvement over ClausIE may be due to factors other than minimization (implicit extractions, different CoreNLP version), showing awareness of confounding factors.
The paper commits to releasing code, datasets, labels, and guidelines, supporting reproducibility and enabling future research.
The paper does not claim to fully minimize extractions in all cases, acknowledging that minimization is 'inherently limited in scope due to the absence of domain knowledge'.

Overall transparency is good: the paper is honest about limitations and does not overstate capabilities. However, transparency is limited by the absence of quantitative analysis of many acknowledged limitations.
epistemic_limits: Formal definition of 'overly specific': The paper relies on intuitive linguistic judgment rather than formal definition. No semantic equivalence metric is provided to validate that removed constituents are truly 'overly specific'. This limits the generalizability of the approach to new domains.

Meaning preservation validation: The paper asserts that annotations preserve meaning but provides no formal validation. No semantic equivalence metrics, entailment-based evaluation, or downstream task validation is provided. This is a critical assumption that is never tested.

Negation detection scope: The paper explicitly limits negation detection to relation-level negations via a simple lexicon. The frequency of unhandled negation cases (scope, focus, double negation) is not quantified. The impact on downstream tasks is unknown.
Modality representation: The paper uses binary CT/PS modality distinction, acknowledging that more nuanced approaches exist. Information loss from this simplification is not analyzed.
Attribution detection completeness: The paper limits attribution detection to subordinate clauses and 'according to' patterns. Other attribution sources may be missed. Completeness is not evaluated.
Redundancy definition: The paper uses simplistic subsequence-based redundancy definition. Semantic redundancy (paraphrases, near-duplicates) is not captured. Recall metrics may be misleading.

Statistical significance: Precision evaluation is limited to small labeled samples (200 sentences) without statistical significance testing. Differences between systems may not be statistically significant.
Attribution precision reliability: Attribution precision is evaluated on sparse data (most sentences lack attributions). Reliability and generalizability are unclear.
Frequency threshold justification: The frequency threshold (≥10) for MinIE-F appears arbitrary. No sensitivity analysis is provided. Impact of threshold choice on different domains is unknown.
Collocation dictionary coverage: The collocation dictionary (WordNet + Wiktionary) may miss domain-specific collocations. Error frequency is not quantified.
Downstream task utility: The paper does not evaluate whether minimized extractions with annotations improve performance on downstream tasks. Practical utility is asserted but not demonstrated.
Dependency parsing error impact: The paper acknowledges that dependency parsing errors propagate through the pipeline but does not quantify their frequency or impact.
Clause-based extraction limitations: The paper focuses on individual clauses, potentially missing cross-clause relations. Performance on complex sentences is not evaluated.
Extraction length as minimality proxy: The paper uses word count as a proxy for minimality but does not validate that word count correlates with semantic minimality.

Negative polarity claim validation: The paper claims negative polarity annotations address a 'critical gap' but provides no empirical demonstration that prior systems lack negative evidence or downstream validation that negative polarity annotations improve reasoning.
Novelty assessment: The novelty of the contribution is subjective and depends on evaluation criteria. Reviewers differ on whether the combination of techniques represents sufficient novelty.
Generalizability: The evaluation is limited to English text from news and Wikipedia. Generalizability to other languages, domains, and text types is unknown.
Annotation correctness: The paper provides coverage statistics for annotations but does not evaluate annotation correctness. Inter-annotator agreement is not reported.

Minimization contribution isolation: The precision improvement of MinIE-S over ClausIE may be due to factors other than minimization (implicit extractions, different CoreNLP version). The minimization contribution is not isolated via ablation study.

Redundancy consolidation causality: The paper claims minimization consolidates redundancy but does not establish causality. Minimization may merely reveal pre-existing redundancy rather than cause consolidation.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: MinIE presents a methodologically sound engineering contribution to open information extraction that systematically addresses extraction minimization through constituent removal and annotation-based representation. The paper addresses a genuine problem (overly-specific extractions obscuring semantic equivalence) with a principled multi-mode architecture (Safe/Frequency/Collocations/Aggressive) that enables tunable trade-offs between extraction brevity and precision. The annotation framework (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) is comprehensive and extends prior work (OLLIE), with negative polarity representation being novel for OIE systems. Empirical evaluation on multiple datasets (NYT-10k, NYT, Wiki) demonstrates consistent improvements in extraction length (7.2±4.2 to 4.7±1.9 words) and competitive precision (MinIE-S 0.79 vs ClausIE 0.68 on NYT). However, the contribution is fundamentally incremental rather than disruptive: individual minimization techniques are largely domain-adaptations of existing ideas (lexicon-based negation detection, frequency-based minimization from ReVerb, clause-based extraction from ClausIE, factuality representation from Saurí & Pustejovsky 2012). The paper exhibits significant methodological limitations: (1) precision evaluation on small labeled samples (200 sentences) without statistical significance testing; (2) core assumptions about linguistic phenomenon detection acknowledged as handling only 'easy cases' with unquantified impact; (3) simplistic redundancy definition (subsequence matching) potentially misrepresenting recall metrics; (4) absence of downstream task evaluation validating practical utility; (5) overstated claims regarding negative polarity as addressing a 'critical gap' (only 3.7% coverage, no downstream validation). The paper's transparency about limitations is a significant strength, but this transparency also reveals the incremental and narrowly-scoped nature of the contribution. Overall, the work is technically competent and suitable for publication at a venue focused on methodological contributions, but would benefit from addressing major methodological concerns before acceptance at a top-tier venue.
strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical relevance: The paper identifies a genuine problem in OIE (overly-specific extractions obscuring semantic equivalence) and provides compelling examples (Table 1) demonstrating the issue across multiple systems.

Comprehensive annotation framework extending prior work: MinIE introduces a structured annotation scheme (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) that is more expressive than prior work (OLLIE). Negative polarity representation is novel for OIE systems, though coverage is limited (3.7%).

Principled multi-mode architecture with explicit trade-offs: The four-mode design (Safe/Frequency/Collocations/Aggressive) is well-motivated and enables users to select trade-offs between extraction brevity and precision. Each mode has clear operational criteria.

Empirical validation on multiple datasets with consistent improvements: Evaluation on NYT-10k, NYT, and Wiki datasets shows consistent improvements in extraction length and competitive precision across datasets. MinIE-S achieves higher precision than ClausIE (0.79 vs 0.68 on NYT) while producing significantly shorter extractions (7.2±4.2 vs 10.9±7 words).

Transparent acknowledgment of limitations and scope boundaries: The paper explicitly identifies limitations (negation scope/focus/double negation not handled, modality uses binary CT/PS, attribution limited to subordinate clauses and 'according to' patterns, clause-based extraction may miss cross-clause relations). This transparency strengthens credibility.

Reproducibility commitment with code and data release: Authors commit to releasing source code, datasets, extractions, labels, and labeling guidelines, supporting reproducibility and enabling future research.

Systematic handling of linguistic phenomena: The paper provides a principled approach to identifying and removing overly-specific constituents while preserving semantic information through annotations. Relation enrichment (Section 4.1) is more principled than prior pattern-based approaches.

Clear presentation and logical flow: The paper is well-organized with clear progression from motivation to related work to overview to detailed techniques to evaluation. Use of examples (Table 1) effectively illustrates concepts.
limitations: Lack of formal definition of 'overly specific': The paper relies on intuitive linguistic judgment to define 'overly specific' constituents but provides no formal definition or semantic equivalence metric. This makes the core concept imprecise and difficult to generalize. The decision of what is 'overly specific' is based on heuristics (e.g., 'universally safe' in MinIE-S, frequency threshold in MinIE-F) without formal criteria.

Annotation scheme sufficiency not validated: The paper asserts that annotations preserve meaning of removed constituents but provides no formal validation. No semantic equivalence metrics, entailment-based evaluation, or downstream task validation is provided. This is a critical assumption that is never tested. The paper does not evaluate whether downstream tasks can recover original meaning from annotations.

Negation detection limited to 'easy cases' with unquantified impact: Negation detection is explicitly limited to relation-level negations via a simple lexicon {no, not, never, none}. The paper acknowledges that negation scope, focus, and double negation are not handled but does not quantify the frequency of missed negations or their impact on downstream tasks. Coverage is low (3.7%), raising questions about whether this represents true negation frequency or detection limitations.

Precision evaluation on small labeled samples without statistical significance testing: Precision is evaluated on only 200-sentence samples (NYT, Wiki) without statistical significance testing or confidence intervals. Differences between systems (e.g., MinIE-S 0.79 vs ClausIE 0.68) may not be statistically significant given the small sample size. No error bars or confidence intervals are provided.

Simplistic redundancy definition potentially misrepresenting recall metrics: Redundancy is defined as subsequence matching ('t1 redundant if it appears as subsequence in some other triple t2'). This definition captures only syntactic redundancy and misses semantic redundancy (paraphrases, near-duplicates, synonymous relations). Recall metrics based on this definition may be misleading, and the claim that MinIE consolidates redundancy is not independently verified.
open_questions: Does minimized extraction with annotations actually preserve semantic meaning? The paper asserts meaning preservation but provides no formal validation. Can downstream tasks (IR, QA, KB extension) recover original meaning from annotations? Would downstream task evaluation demonstrate that minimized extractions are as useful as original extractions?

How frequently are negations missed due to scope, focus, and double negation limitations? The paper acknowledges these cases are not handled but does not quantify their frequency in the evaluation datasets. What is the false negative rate of negation detection? How would more sophisticated negation detection (e.g., scope resolution) improve coverage and downstream task performance?

Is the precision improvement of MinIE-S over ClausIE (0.79 vs 0.68) attributable to minimization or confounding factors? Authors acknowledge that improvement may be due to 'additional high-precision implicit extractions, breaks up very long and thus error-prone extractions, and uses a different version of Stanford CoreNLP' (line 773-776). Would an ablation study isolating the contribution of minimization show similar improvements?

Do negative polarity annotations actually address a 'critical gap' in prior OIE systems? The paper claims this but provides no empirical demonstration that prior systems cannot represent negations or downstream validation that negative polarity annotations improve reasoning tasks. Would downstream task evaluation (KB extension, QA) demonstrate that negative polarity annotations improve performance?

How robust is the approach to hyperparameter choices? The frequency threshold (≥10) for MinIE-F appears arbitrary. How sensitive are results to this choice? Would different thresholds (5, 15, 20) produce significantly different results? How would domain-specific collocation dictionaries affect MinIE-C performance?

What is the impact of dependency parsing errors on MinIE precision? The paper acknowledges that parsing errors are the main source of errors in MinIE-S but does not quantify their frequency or impact. Would evaluation on gold-standard parses show how much of MinIE's error is due to parsing vs. minimization?

Does clause-based extraction miss important cross-clause relations? The paper focuses on individual clauses, potentially missing cross-clause relations. How would performance on complex multi-clause sentences compare to single-clause sentences? Would extending MinIE to handle cross-clause relations significantly improve recall?

Is word count a valid proxy for minimality? The paper uses mean word count as a proxy for minimality but does not validate that word count correlates with semantic minimality. Would human evaluation of semantic minimality show that shorter extractions are actually more minimal? Are there alternative minimality metrics that better capture the intended concept?
consensus_snapshot: MinIE addresses a genuine problem in OIE: overly-specific extractions that obscure semantic equivalence and complicate downstream tasks.
The annotation framework (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) is comprehensive and extends prior work (OLLIE). Negative polarity representation is novel for OIE systems.
The multi-mode architecture (Safe/Frequency/Collocations/Aggressive) is well-motivated and principled, enabling users to select trade-offs between extraction brevity and precision.
Empirical evaluation on multiple datasets shows consistent improvements in extraction length and competitive precision.
The paper demonstrates intellectual honesty by explicitly acknowledging limitations and scope boundaries.
Individual minimization techniques are largely domain-adaptations of existing ideas. Novelty is primarily in the combination and systematic application.
The paper lacks downstream task evaluation validating that minimized extractions with annotations improve performance on IR, QA, or KB extension tasks.
The paper's transparency about limitations is a significant strength, but this transparency also reveals the incremental and narrowly-scoped nature of the contribution.
disagreement_snapshot: Reviewers differ on the significance of the negative polarity contribution. Some view it as addressing a documented gap; others view the claim as overstated given low coverage (3.7%) and lack of downstream validation. The representation is adapted from Saurí & Pustejovsky (2012), making the novelty primarily in application scope rather than conceptual innovation.

Reviewers differ on whether the precision improvement of MinIE-S over ClausIE is attributable to minimization or confounding factors (implicit extractions, different CoreNLP version). The minimization contribution is unclear without ablation study.

Reviewers differ on novelty assessment. Incremental novelty lens views MinIE as a well-executed refinement; disruptive novelty lens views it as fundamentally incremental. The distinction depends on evaluation criteria and venue expectations.

Reviewers differ on the severity of the simplistic redundancy definition. Some view it as a major methodological flaw that misrepresents recall metrics; others treat it as a limitation but not fundamental.

Reviewers differ on the importance of statistical significance testing. Some emphasize the lack of significance tests on small samples as a major flaw; others note this is common practice in OIE research due to annotation costs.
uncertainty_snapshot: Meaning preservation claim: The paper asserts that annotations preserve meaning but provides no formal validation. No semantic equivalence metrics or downstream task validation is provided. This is a critical assumption that is never tested.

Negation detection scope and impact: The paper limits negation detection to 'easy cases' and acknowledges that scope, focus, and double negation are not handled. However, the frequency of missed negations and their impact on downstream tasks is not quantified.

Negative polarity claim as addressing 'critical gap': The paper claims negative polarity annotations address a critical gap, but evidence is weak: only 3.7% coverage, no empirical demonstration that prior systems lack negative evidence, and no downstream validation.

Statistical significance of precision improvements: Precision is evaluated on small labeled samples (200 sentences) without statistical significance testing. Differences between systems may not be statistically significant.
Redundancy definition and recall metrics: Redundancy is defined as subsequence matching, which may miss semantic redundancy. Recall metrics may be misleading.
Downstream task utility: The paper motivates the work with downstream tasks but does not evaluate on these tasks. Practical utility is asserted but not demonstrated.
Novelty assessment: Reviewers differ on whether MinIE's contribution is sufficiently novel. The distinction between 'incremental' and 'disruptive' is subjective.

Precision improvement attribution: MinIE-S achieves higher precision than ClausIE, but authors acknowledge this may be due to implicit extractions, breaking up long extractions, and different CoreNLP version. The minimization contribution is unclear.

human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: MinIE presents a methodologically sound engineering contribution to OIE that systematically addresses extraction minimization through constituent removal and annotation-based representation. The paper's core claims are largely supported by evidence, though with important caveats regarding scope, formalization, and validation. The primary decision points are: (1) Whether the engineering contribution (multi-mode design, comprehensive annotation framework) is sufficiently novel and impactful for the target venue; (2) Whether the methodological limitations (small labeled samples without statistical significance testing, absence of downstream task evaluation, simplistic redundancy definition) are acceptable or require major revisions; (3) Whether the overstated claims (particularly regarding negative polarity as addressing a 'critical gap') should be toned down or require additional evidence. The paper is suitable for publication at a venue focused on methodological contributions (e.g., ACL, EMNLP) but would benefit from addressing major methodological concerns before acceptance at a top-tier venue. Recommended actions: (1) Conduct downstream task evaluation on at least one task (IR, QA, KB extension) to validate practical utility; (2) Report confidence intervals and statistical significance tests on precision differences; (3) Revise negative polarity claim to be more modest; (4) Provide error analysis quantifying the impact of acknowledged limitations. The paper's transparency about limitations is a significant strength that should be preserved.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: The paper makes solid contributions to OIE but would be strengthened by: (1) Downstream task evaluation: Evaluate MinIE on IR, QA, or KB extension tasks. Compare performance using minimized extractions with annotations to baseline extractions. This would validate practical utility and strengthen motivation. (2) Statistical rigor: Report 95% confidence intervals for all precision estimates. Conduct statistical significance tests (e.g., McNemar's test) to compare systems. Consider increasing labeled sample size or using cross-validation. (3) Negation detection: Quantify the frequency of unhandled negation cases (scope, focus, double negation) in evaluation datasets. Provide error analysis showing false negatives. Consider implementing more sophisticated negation detection. (4) Redundancy analysis: Extend redundancy definition to capture semantic redundancy (paraphrases, near-duplicates). Conduct manual analysis of redundant extractions. Re-evaluate recall metrics using semantic redundancy definition. (5) Meaning preservation: Conduct human evaluation to verify that (minimized extraction + annotations) conveys the same information as original extraction. Measure inter-annotator agreement on annotation correctness. (6) Revise claims: Tone down the claim about negative polarity addressing a 'critical gap' to be more modest. Provide empirical evidence that prior OIE systems cannot represent negations or conduct downstream task evaluation validating that negative polarity annotations improve performance. (7) Sensitivity analysis: Conduct sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters (frequency threshold for MinIE-F, collocation dictionary sources, negation lexicon). Provide guidance on parameter selection for different applications. (8) Error analysis: Quantify the frequency of dependency parsing errors, collocation handling errors, and NER failures in evaluation datasets. Analyze the impact of each error source on MinIE precision. (9) Annotation validation: Report inter-annotator agreement metrics for the annotation scheme. Evaluate annotation correctness, not just coverage. (10) Clarify novelty: Explicitly clarify which contributions are novel vs. incremental. Emphasize the combination of techniques and the systematic application of minimization across multiple linguistic phenomena.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: when an un- usual entity pair (Selena, Norway) is suddenly seen in three articles on a single day: Selena traveled to Norway to see her ex-boyfriend. Selena arrived in Norway for a rendezvous with Justin. Selena’s trip to Norway was no coincidence. It is likely that all three refer to the same event re- lation, travel-to(person, location)1, and can be used as positive training examples for the relation. As in Zhang & Weld (2013), we group parallel sentences sharing the same argument pair and date in a struc- ture called a NewsSpike. However, we include all sentences mentioning the arguments ( e.g. Selena’s trip to Norway ) in the NewsSpike (not just those yielding OpenIE extractions), and use the lexical- ized dependency path between the arguments ( e.g. <-[poss]-trip-[prep-to]->2, as the event phrase. In this way, we can generalize extractors beyond the scope of OpenIE. Formally, a NewsSpike is a tu- ple, (a1,a 2,d,S ), where a1 and a2 are arguments (e.g. Selena),d is a date, andS is a set of argument- labeled sentences{(s,a 1,a 2,p )...}in whichs is a sentence with argumentsai and event phrasep. Conclusion LODIE is a project that addresses complex challenges that we believe are novel and of high interest to the scientific community. It is timely because for the first time in the history of IE a very large-scale informa - tion resource is available, covering a growing number of domains and of the very recent interest in the use of linked data for web extraction. While the LODIE project as a whole tackles diverse challenges, in this article we focused on how to obtain training data from the LOD and use them for an IE task. top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: Articles SPRING 2015 55 E xtracting information from a gigantic data source such as the web has been considered a major research chal- lenge, and over the years many different approaches (Etzioni et al. 2004; Banko et al. 2007; Carlson et al. 2010; Freedman and Ramshaw 2011; Nakashole, Theobald, and Weikum 2011) have been proposed. Nevertheless, the current state of the art has mainly addressed tasks for which resources for training are available (for example, the TAP ontology in the paper by Etzioni and colleagues [2004]) or use generic patterns to extract generic facts (for example, Banko et al. [2007]; OpenCalais.com). The limited availability of resources for training has so far prevented the study of the generalized use of large-scale resources to port to specific user information needs. The linked open data information-extrac - tion (LODIE) project focuses on the study of IE models and algorithms able to perform efficient user-centered web-scale learning by exploiting linked open data (LOD). Content: data for research? After the review process is completed, anonymized review data can be provided to the research community, given the consent of the willing reviewers and authors. ARR implemented a framework for proactive data collection from the willing reviewers and authors agreeing to contribute it. We hope that you would consider opting in. This is done in the form where you set your availability for review cycles. The more data we have, the more we can do as NLP experts to improve peer review. What about the author anonymity? While ACL has replaced the embargo period with other measures to incentivize anonymity, the reviewing guidelines are as follows: To preserve the merits of double-blind review, reviewers for *ACL conferences and TACL should be instructed not to actively try to discover the identity of the authors and not to let any suspicion or knowledge of author identity affect their judgment of the paper. This should not prevent them from searching for related work, but they should take special care and postpone such searches until after they have read the paper completely and formed an initial impression of it. If a reviewer nevertheless uncovers the identity of the authors (or believes they can identify the authors for other reasons), they should inform the area chair or action editor (but not other reviewers) so that this information can be taken into account when making the final acceptance decision.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

The exponential growth of the web generates an exceptional quan - tity of data for which automatic knowl- edge capture is essential. This work describes the methodology for web-scale information extraction in the linked open data information-extraction (LODIE) project and highlights results from the early experiments carried out in the initial phase of the project. LODIE aims to develop information- extraction techniques able to scale at web level and adapt to user information needs. The core idea behind LODIE is the usage of linked open data, a very large-scale information resource, as a ground-breaking solution for IE, which provides invaluable annotated data on a growing number of domains. Conclusion LODIE is a project that addresses complex challenges that we believe are novel and of high interest to the scientific community. It is timely because for the first time in the history of IE a very large-scale informa - tion resource is available, covering a growing number of domains and of the very recent interest in the use of linked data for web extraction. While the LODIE project as a whole tackles diverse challenges, in this article we focused on how to obtain training data from the LOD and use them for an IE task. We exper - imented with the use of linked data dictionaries to automatically generate annotations for learning. The generated annotations, despite the presence of noise, are valuable for certain tasks. Hallucinated references or citations: Please check carefully for hallucinated references, which pose a serious concern to scientific reliability. Anonymity violations. As of January 2024, non-anonymous pre-prints are permitted for ARR, but submissions should still be properly anonymized (e.g., not containing explicit references to the authors’ prior work, acknowledgements, links to non-anonymous repositories or services like Dropbox that may track who opened the link). Style guides or length violations: the paper should be desk-rejected if it does not follow the style guides or goes over the page limit (4 pages for short, 8 for long papers, excluding the ethical considerations and limitations).

top_documents.title: Document 3
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: As a counter to common problems with reviews, there are also common problems with NLP papers. We do ask you to watch out for these and point them out when you see them. Above all else, published research should at least be technically sound and appropriately scoped. As with the above reviewer issues, it’s a case-by-case evaluation: some things in the list below may be appropriate in a given context, given that they are sufficiently motivated. We provide codes for different types of issues (e.g. M1, G2…) that can be referenced in discussions.
